Volvo's New Factory Worker Is Wheeled and Still in Training
53 photos
Photo: Volvo
Volvo's Ghent facility prepares to welcome a new kind of worker. 1.65 meters (5 feet 5 inches) tall, the AEON humanoid robot weighs 60 kilograms (132 pounds), moves around on wheels, and carries loads no heavier than 10 kilos (22 pounds). For the time being, the newcomer is learning to put components into two fixtures. The kicker here is that humans are teaching it how.
Hardly the automated revolution promised by some of the industry's more enthusiastic futurists, with Elon Musk and the Optimus Gen 3 coming to mind. Volvo, however, wants AEON to become a useful addition to its Ghent complex in Belgium. Developed by Hexagon Robotics, the humanoid robot will specialize in repetitive jobs and physically demanding tasks.
Production use is targeted from the middle of 2027, following a pilot in the first half of next year. Volvo's announcement is a bit awkward, though. Back in October 2026, the Swedish manufacturer confirmed 2,500 job reductions worldwide after reporting a particularly miserable third quarter.
Revenue fell 22.6 percent year over year, with the company recording an operating loss of SEK 5.6 billion while burning through SEK 8.9 billion in free cash flow. Adding insult to injury, Volvo Cars also needs to find another SEK 5 billion in savings. Bringing humanoid workers into production is a hard-to-miss juxtaposition, but robots won't replace human workers anytime soon.
The October 2026 job reductions announcement targets white-collar roles, namely administrative, office, engineering, and management staff rather than production line workers. Alongside the 2,500 white-collar job cuts reported in the Q3 2026 financial update, Volvo stated that it's adapting the blue-collar workforce to match lower sales volumes. Reading between the lines, Volvo has probably made a small bet on reducing a part of its production costs with a bunch of robots.
Photo: Volvo Pretending these announcements have nothing to do with the pressure to reduce manufacturing costs would be naive. Speaking of, there is a wider manufacturing rethink underway. As part of the Q3 2026 financial update, Volvo made it clear that it's concentrating production in five dedicated plants globally.
Volvo is also exploring multi-brand assembly operations with Geely at the Belgian plant and in Chengdu, China. As you're well aware, Geely is the Chinese colossus that calls the shots at Volvo Cars nowadays. Zhejiang Geely Holding Group is presently listed as holding nearly 79 percent of the shares.
Geely owned 100 percent of Volvo Cars between August 2010 and October 2021, with Ford selling the Swedish automaker for a puny USD 1.8 billion. The Chinese overlord reduced its ownership to 82 percent in October 2021, then to 79 in November 2023. On both occasions, it did it to improve stock liquidity while funding growth.
Turning our attention back to the wheeled robots from Ghent, the argument here is that certain factory jobs are better suited for robots, who are particularly good at doing the same operation repeatedly. Auto factories already have plenty of robots, albeit not humanoid. Think industrial arms designed to weld, paint, lift, and install components fast.
The human proportions of the AEON robot allow it to interact with the existing assembly plant environment, while its wheeled base provides mobility, making more sense than legs for much of the factory's floor. Nevertheless, the AEON robot wouldn't mean anything if Volvo employees don't demonstrate tasks to it, allowing the robot to learn how to reproduce those tasks consistently.
After placing components accurately into two fixtures, the humanoid worker will be taught to handle multiple components, navigate the production area, and communicate with the factory's automated systems. In TL;DR form, Volvo is effectively asking Ghent personnel to teach a new colleague how to do a variety of jobs before deciding how much of that work the robot can take on.
